patient.name: Priya Raman
patient.setting: GP surgery, then neurology and the Emergency Department
patient.complaint: Drooping eyelids and double vision that get worse through the day
background: Pharmacist in Wembley; mother of one
Recently started propranolol for performance anxiety

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with fatigable ptosis and diplopia worse in the evening, normal reflexes and sensation. Distractors: Lambert-Eaton, MS, motor neurone disease, GBS, third nerve palsy. Also asked: which drug made it worse, and myasthenic crisis.

points: Priya, 31: eyelids droop by **evening**; fine in the morning.
Double vision when reading late; chewing tires her at dinner.
Lifting her toddler is hard by the end of the day.

steps.lead: Weakness that is **fatigable** (worse with use, better with rest) and hits the eyes first is the signature of myasthenia: **ptosis and diplopia**, worse at the end of the day.

points: Sustained upgaze for 60 s: right lid droops further.
Shoulder abduction weakens on repeated testing.

steps.lead: Pure motor, fatigable weakness with normal reflexes, sensation and pupils localises to the **neuromuscular junction**: IgG antibodies against the postsynaptic ACh receptor.

steps.q: Priya's weakness worsens with repeated use and her reflexes are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: **Myasthenia gravis**: fatigable, ocular-first, normal reflexes. LEMS improves with repeated effort and has reduced reflexes.

steps.lead: Priya also has **hypothyroidism**: myasthenia clusters with other autoimmune disease. A **thymoma** must be looked for; **MuSK** antibody disease is more severe.

steps.text: Priya's new **propranolol** may be unmasking her weakness. Beta-blockers, aminoglycosides, macrolides, antimalarials and lithium all worsen myasthenia.

steps.lead: Her propranolol is stopped. If she ever has surgery, the anaesthetist must know: she will be **resistant to suxamethonium**.

points: A year later: chest infection; a walk-in centre gives **clarithromycin**.
Two days on: breathless, weak cough, slurred speech.
Cannot count to 20 in one breath.

steps.lead: Priya is in **myasthenic crisis**: respiratory muscle weakness, a **bovine cough** and risk of type II respiratory failure. The macrolide was the trigger.

steps.text: SpO2 stays normal until late in neuromuscular respiratory failure. A falling **FVC** warns you first.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (AChR antibodies), the next test once diagnosed (CT chest for thymoma), and 'Which is the best way to monitor her breathing?' (FVC) in crisis.

steps.q: Priya has fatigable ptosis and diplopia. Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
steps.r: **Serum AChR antibodies** first (plus anti-MuSK if negative). CK is normal in myasthenia; MRI and LP look for other causes.

steps.title: Priya's neuromuscular screen
steps.text: Strongly positive AChR antibodies confirm myasthenia. A normal CK argues against a myopathy.

steps.lead: Priya's positive **AChR antibodies** are the first test. **Repetitive nerve stimulation** would show a **decrement**; the Tensilon test is historic.

visual.title: Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz
visual.caption: A **decremental** response (>10% fall by the 4th to 5th stimulus) is the EMG sign of myasthenia.

steps.lead: Once diagnosed, Priya has a **CT chest** to look for a **thymoma** in the anterior mediastinum.

points: CT chest: a 3 cm anterior mediastinal mass.

steps.lead: In her crisis, Priya's breathing is tracked with **FVC**, the gold standard for respiratory effort. Saturations and ABG change late.

visual.title: Priya's FVC in crisis
visual.caption: Falling FVC with normal-looking saturations: she needs ICU review before her gases fail.

steps.text: Do not reassure on an SpO2 of 93%. In myasthenic crisis **FVC**, not oxygen saturation, tells you how close she is to ventilation.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (pyridostigmine), the next step for persistent symptoms (prednisolone and/or azathioprine), thymoma (thymectomy) and crisis (respiratory support plus IVIG or plasma exchange).

steps.q: Priya's diagnosis is confirmed. Which is the first-line drug?
steps.r: **Pyridostigmine**, a long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is first line for symptoms.

steps.lead: Priya starts **pyridostigmine**: more ACh in the cleft, better strength, quickly.

points: Three months on: still ptosis by evening despite full-dose pyridostigmine.
Diarrhoea and cramps limit further increases.

steps.lead: Persistent symptoms on pyridostigmine mean adding immunosuppression: **prednisolone and/or azathioprine** (azathioprine is the steroid-sparing agent).
Priya's CT showed a **thymoma**, so she is listed for **thymectomy**, the definitive treatment.

steps.title: Myasthenia gravis: stepwise treatment
nodes: Crisis: ventilate if needed + IVIG or plasma exchange

visual.title: FVC in myasthenic crisis
visual.label: Priya 1.0 L = 15 mL/kg
visual.caption: Priya weighs 65 kg; 1.0 L is about 15 mL/kg, below the usual 20 mL/kg trigger for ventilation.

steps.lead: Priya is admitted to ICU for **respiratory support**, then given **IV immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis** to clear the antibodies. The clarithromycin is stopped.

steps.text: In crisis, do not just push up pyridostigmine. Airway and breathing first, then **IVIG or plasma exchange**.
Steroids can cause a transient **worsening** of myasthenia when first started, so they are begun at a low dose and increased.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: the hypersensitivity type and target (type II, postsynaptic nicotinic AChR), why weakness is fatigable, how pyridostigmine works, and why thymectomy helps.

steps.title: What goes wrong at the junction
nodes: End-plate potential fails with repeated firing
steps.caption: A type II hypersensitivity against a receptor.

steps.lead: Priya's antibodies are a **type II hypersensitivity**: they bind, internalise and complement-destroy her postsynaptic receptors.

steps.q: Which type of hypersensitivity is myasthenia gravis?
steps.r: **Type II**: IgG against a fixed cell-surface antigen (the AChR). Graves' is also type II.

steps.lead: Each repeated contraction releases less ACh; with too few receptors, the signal falls below threshold. That is why Priya is **fine in the morning and weak at night**.
**Pyridostigmine** blocks acetylcholinesterase, so ACh lingers in the cleft and finds the receptors that remain.
Had Priya been **MuSK**-positive, her receptors would fail to **cluster**, a different mechanism with more bulbar and respiratory weakness.
Removing Priya's **thymoma** removes a driver of autoantibody production: why thymectomy works.

steps.text: Pyridostigmine's side effects (diarrhoea, cramps, salivation) are **muscarinic**. Too much can cause a **cholinergic crisis** with worsening weakness.

mcq.q: What is the classic pattern of weakness in myasthenia gravis?
o: Fatigable, worse at end of day
mcq.r: **Fatigable** weakness, ocular first, worse in the evening. Improvement with effort is LEMS.

mcq.q: Which tumour is associated with myasthenia gravis?
mcq.r: **Thymoma**. Small cell lung cancer is linked to Lambert-Eaton.

mcq.q: Which drug can worsen myasthenia gravis?
mcq.r: **Aminoglycosides**, macrolides, beta-blockers, antimalarials and lithium worsen MG.

mcq.q: Which antibody is linked to a more severe, progressive form?
mcq.r: **MuSK** antibodies: more bulbar and respiratory involvement.

mcq.q: What is the initial investigation for suspected myasthenia?
What does repetitive nerve stimulation show in myasthenia?
How is respiratory effort monitored in myasthenic crisis?
mcq.r: **FVC** is the gold standard; saturations fall late.

mcq.q: What is the first-line drug for myasthenia gravis?
Which is a definitive treatment for myasthenic crisis?
Which receptor do the antibodies in myasthenia gravis target?

points.p: IgG antibodies against postsynaptic ACh receptors at the NMJ

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the classic distractor pair.

points.p: MG: postsynaptic AChR; LEMS: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
MG worsens with repeated use; LEMS briefly improves
MG: normal reflexes; LEMS: reduced reflexes
MG: thymoma; LEMS: small cell lung cancer

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: known MG + breathless = crisis until proven otherwise.

points.p: Triggers: infection and drugs (aminoglycosides, macrolides, beta-blockers)
points.why: Look for a new drug in the stem.

prompts.q: Which drugs worsen myasthenia, and what is the anaesthetic issue?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'most likely cause of deterioration' question.

points.why: A slow pulse in the stem is a hint.
They are sensitive to non-depolarising blockers.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always look for the thymus.

points.why: CT chest for all new cases.

points.p: MuSK antibodies: more severe, bulbar, progressive

prompts.q: Which investigations confirm myasthenia, and what is done next?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: antibodies first, then a CT chest.

points.p: Tensilon (edrophonium) test is historic: cardiac risk
points.why: Not the answer for a modern initial test.

prompts.q: How do you monitor breathing in myasthenic crisis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: SpO2 is falsely reassuring.

prompts.q: What is the stepwise treatment of myasthenia gravis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: symptomatic, then immunosuppression, then thymus.

prompts.q: How do you manage a myasthenic crisis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: airway first, then remove the antibodies.

points.p: Admit; respiratory support, may need intubation and ventilation
Stop the trigger drug, treat infection

prompts.q: Explain the pathophysiology of myasthenia and why it is fatigable.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the hypersensitivity type and the receptor.

points.p: IgG binds postsynaptic nicotinic AChR: internalisation and complement damage
Repeated firing depletes ACh relative to the reduced receptors: fatigue
points.why: Hence worse at the end of the day.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one is symptomatic, one targets the antibody source.

Thymus (hyperplasia or thymoma) drives autoantibody production

glossary.Myasthenia gravis: Autoimmune disease where antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable weakness.
glossary.NMJ: Neuromuscular junction: the synapse between a motor nerve and a muscle fibre.
glossary.neuromuscular junction: The synapse where a motor nerve releases acetylcholine onto muscle.
glossary.AChR: Acetylcholine receptor; the nicotinic receptor on the muscle end-plate targeted in myasthenia.
glossary.Acetylcholine receptor antibodies: Serum IgG against the AChR; the first test for myasthenia.
glossary.MuSK: Muscle-specific tyrosine kinase; antibodies against it cause a more severe, bulbar form of myasthenia.
glossary.Fatigable: Weakness that worsens with repeated or sustained use and recovers with rest.
glossary.Bulbar: Muscles of speech, chewing and swallowing, supplied by the brainstem.
glossary.Myasthenic crisis: Life-threatening respiratory and bulbar weakness in myasthenia needing urgent respiratory support.
glossary.Bovine cough: A weak, breathy cough from inability to close the vocal cords or generate force.
glossary.Type II respiratory failure: Low oxygen with a raised carbon dioxide from inadequate ventilation.
glossary.Cholinergic crisis: Weakness, sweating, salivation and diarrhoea from too much acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.
glossary.Thymoma: A tumour of the thymus in the anterior mediastinum, linked to myasthenia.
glossary.Thymus: Gland in the anterior mediastinum where T cells mature; drives antibody production in myasthenia.
glossary.Thymectomy: Surgical removal of the thymus; definitive treatment in myasthenia, especially with thymoma.
glossary.Anterior mediastinum: The front part of the space between the lungs, where the thymus sits.
glossary.Lambert-Eaton: Lambert-Eaton syndrome: presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, often with small cell lung cancer; strength improves with effort.
glossary.VGCC: Voltage-gated calcium channel; the presynaptic target in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
glossary.Repetitive nerve stimulation: EMG test firing a nerve repeatedly; myasthenia shows a falling (decremental) response.
glossary.Decremental response: Progressive fall in muscle response with repeated nerve stimulation, typical of myasthenia.
glossary.EMG: Electromyography: recording of muscle electrical activity.
glossary.Tensilon test: Historic test giving IV edrophonium to see if weakness briefly improves; rarely used due to cardiac risk.
glossary.Edrophonium: Very short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in the historic Tensilon test.
glossary.FVC: Forced vital capacity: the volume breathed out forcefully after a full breath; monitors respiratory muscle strength.
glossary.Pyridostigmine: Long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; first-line symptomatic treatment for myasthenia.
glossary.Acetylcholinesterase: Enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft.
glossary.Azathioprine: Immunosuppressant used as a steroid-sparing agent in myasthenia.
glossary.Prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid used for persistent myasthenia symptoms.
glossary.IVIG: Intravenous immunoglobulin: pooled antibodies that dampen the autoimmune attack in crisis.
glossary.Plasmapheresis: Plasma exchange: removing the patient's plasma to clear circulating antibodies.
glossary.Suxamethonium: Depolarising muscle relaxant used in anaesthesia; myasthenic patients are resistant to it.
glossary.Aminoglycosides: Antibiotics such as gentamicin that impair neuromuscular transmission and worsen myasthenia.
glossary.Macrolides: Antibiotics such as clarithromycin that can worsen myasthenia.
glossary.Type II hypersensitivity: Antibodies binding a fixed cell-surface antigen, causing damage or blocking function.
glossary.Nicotinic: The acetylcholine receptor type at the neuromuscular junction.
glossary.Internalisation: The cell pulling receptors from its surface inside, reducing the number available.
glossary.Complement: Blood proteins that, once activated by antibody, damage cell membranes.

technique.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 3 month history of double vision and drooping of her left eyelid. Both are worse in the evening and better after sleep. She finds it hard to finish chewing a meal. On sustained upward gaze her left eyelid droops further. Pupils, reflexes and sensation are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about ptosis and diplopia: is it fatigable?

clues: worse in the evening and better after sleep
On sustained upward gaze her left eyelid droops further
Pupils, reflexes and sensation are normal
steps.x: Fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness, pure motor, normal pupils.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myasthenia gravis**.

elim: Horner's ptosis is mild and fixed, with a small pupil.
LEMS affects proximal legs, improves with use and reduces reflexes.
MS is relapsing CNS disease with sensory and UMN signs, not fatigable weakness.
CN III palsy is not fatigable and often has a dilated pupil.

steps.x: **D. Myasthenia gravis.** Fatigable ptosis + diplopia + normal pupils and reflexes = myasthenia.

technique.stem: A 65 year old man with myasthenia gravis is admitted with 2 days of increasing breathlessness and difficulty swallowing. He can count only to 8 in one breath. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor his respiratory function?

steps.x: It asks how to **monitor** respiratory function in a neuromuscular patient.

clues: count only to 8 in one breath
steps.x: Myasthenic crisis; saturations still look acceptable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **FVC**, measured serially.

elim: ABG changes late; hypercapnia means he is already failing.
CXR looks for aspiration but does not measure muscle strength.
Saturations stay normal until late.
Peak flow measures airway obstruction and depends on effort.

steps.x: **C. Forced vital capacity.** Neuromuscular breathing = FVC, not SpO2.

technique.stem: A 40 year old woman with myasthenia gravis has had persistent ptosis and limb weakness for 4 months despite the maximum tolerated dose of pyridostigmine. CT chest shows no thymoma. She has no breathing or swallowing problems.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: Next step after first-line failure, in a stable patient.
Persistent symptoms on pyridostigmine, no crisis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add immunosuppression: **prednisolone** (azathioprine as steroid-sparing).

elim: IVIG is for crisis or severe acute deterioration.
Plasma exchange is also for crisis.
Beta-blockers worsen myasthenia.
Stopping removes her symptomatic treatment.

steps.x: **C. Prednisolone.** Pyridostigmine first; persistent = prednisolone and/or azathioprine.

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman has fatigable ptosis and positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies. She starts pyridostigmine and her strength improves within an hour of each dose.
technique.q: Which is the mechanism of action of this drug?

steps.x: A drug mechanism question.

clues: improves within an hour of each dose
steps.x: Rapid symptomatic effect: it acts at the junction, not on the immune system.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pyridostigmine **inhibits acetylcholinesterase**, so ACh stays longer in the cleft.

elim: That is how non-depolarising muscle relaxants work.
That would reduce ACh release and worsen weakness.
That is plasma exchange.
That is azathioprine or steroids, which take weeks.

steps.x: **C. Inhibits acetylcholinesterase.** Fast and symptomatic = acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 2 month history of drooping eyelids and double vision that is worse at the end of the working day. She has also noticed her voice becoming nasal when she talks for a long time. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Reflexes and sensation are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness with normal reflexes and sensation is myasthenia gravis. LEMS improves with repeated effort and reduces reflexes.

steps.x: Diagnosis: decide whether weakness is fatigable.

clues: worse at the end of the working day
nasal when she talks for a long time
steps.x: Fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness; pure motor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myasthenia gravis**.

elim: GBS is acute, ascending and areflexic.
LEMS improves with use and reduces reflexes.
MND is progressive, not fatigable, with fasciculations and spares the eyes.
Myotonic dystrophy has slow muscle relaxation and is not worse through the day.

steps.x: **D. Myasthenia gravis.** End-of-day ptosis and diplopia = myasthenia.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has a 6 week history of difficulty swallowing at the end of meals and weakness lifting his arms above his head, both of which improve after rest. On examination, shoulder abduction weakens with repeated testing. There are no fasciculations. Reflexes and sensation are normal. Pupils are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fatigable bulbar and proximal weakness that improves with rest and normal reflexes is myasthenia gravis, which has a second peak in older men. MND has fasciculations and is not fatigable.

steps.x: Diagnosis: an older man with bulbar and proximal weakness.
Fatigable bulbar and proximal weakness, no LMN or sensory signs. MG has a second peak in older men.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myasthenia gravis**.

elim: Inclusion body myositis is slowly progressive and not fatigable.
LEMS improves with exercise and has reduced reflexes.
MND would show fasciculations and is not fatigable.
PMR causes stiffness and pain, not true weakness.

steps.x: **D. Myasthenia gravis.** Fatigable weakness is MG at any age.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman with myasthenia gravis has a 1 week history of worsening ptosis and difficulty chewing. Her regular medicines are levothyroxine, omeprazole and amlodipine, and 2 weeks ago she started a new tablet for migraine prevention. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her deterioration?
practice.e: Beta-blockers such as propranolol worsen neuromuscular transmission in myasthenia; the slow pulse fits. Amlodipine and paracetamol are not recognised triggers.

steps.x: It asks which drug caused the deterioration.
Known MG worsening 2 weeks after a new migraine preventer; a slow pulse points to a beta-blocker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Propranolol** (beta-blockers worsen MG).

elim: Amlodipine is not a recognised trigger.
Treating hypothyroidism does not worsen MG.
Omeprazole does not worsen myasthenia.
Paracetamol is safe in myasthenia.

steps.x: **E. Propranolol.** Beta-blockers, aminoglycosides, macrolides, antimalarials, lithium worsen MG.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man with myasthenia gravis has a 2 day history of increasing breathlessness, a weak cough and difficulty swallowing after starting antibiotics for a chest infection. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 142/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Respiratory and bulbar muscle weakness with a weak (bovine) cough in a myasthenic after infection and antibiotics is myasthenic crisis, risking type II respiratory failure.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a known myasthenia patient who is now breathless.
Respiratory and bulbar weakness in MG, triggered by infection and antibiotics (macrolides, aminoglycosides).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myasthenic crisis**.

elim: Asthma gives wheeze; this is a weak, ineffective cough from muscle weakness.
GBS is a new ascending areflexic paralysis, not a known MG patient.
PE does not cause dysphagia and bulbar weakness.
Infection triggered it, but bulbar and respiratory muscle failure is the crisis.

steps.x: **C. Myasthenic crisis.** MG + breathlessness + bulbar weakness = myasthenic crisis.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 4 month history of double vision and drooping eyelids, worse in the evening. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Ptosis increasing on sustained upward gaze
practice.e: Sustained upgaze fatigues the levator, so ptosis increases: the bedside sign of myasthenia. Pupils, reflexes and sensation are normal.

steps.x: Most likely examination finding in confirmed myasthenia.
Confirmed MG: the classic bedside sign is fatigability.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze**.

elim: Reflexes are normal in myasthenia.
Pupils are spared in myasthenia; a dilated pupil suggests CN III.
Tongue fasciculations suggest MND.
Sensation is normal in myasthenia.

steps.x: **E. Ptosis increasing on sustained upward gaze.** MG signs are fatigable; pupils, reflexes and sensation are normal.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has severe weakness of her face, tongue and neck with difficulty swallowing and a nasal voice. Her eyes are only mildly affected. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative.
practice.q: Which antibody is most likely to be positive?
practice.e: AChR-negative myasthenia with prominent bulbar weakness is typical of MuSK antibody disease, which is more severe. VGCC antibodies cause LEMS.

steps.x: Which antibody: seronegative for AChR but a decrement on RNS.

clues: severe weakness of her face, tongue and neck
steps.x: AChR-negative myasthenia with severe bulbar disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anti-MuSK**.

elim: Anti-GM1 is linked to multifocal motor neuropathy.
Anti-NMDA causes encephalitis with psychiatric features.
That is Graves' disease.
VGCC antibodies cause LEMS, which shows an increment, not a decrement.

steps.x: **B. Anti-MuSK.** AChR negative + severe bulbar = MuSK myasthenia.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 6 week history of fatigable ptosis and double vision worse in the evening. Reflexes, sensation and pupils are normal. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Serum AChR antibodies are the first test, with anti-MuSK if negative; repetitive nerve stimulation adds a decrement. The Tensilon test is historic because of cardiac risk.

steps.x: Initial test for suspected myasthenia.

clues: Reflexes, sensation and pupils are normal
steps.x: Classic ocular myasthenia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **AChR antibody screen** (with anti-MuSK).

elim: CK is normal in myasthenia; it is for myopathy.
The Tensilon test is historic, with cardiac risks.
LP is for CNS inflammation or GBS.
MRI excludes brainstem lesions but does not diagnose myasthenia.

steps.x: **A. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies.** Suspected MG = AChR antibodies first.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man has just been diagnosed with myasthenia gravis after a positive acetylcholine receptor antibody test. He is stable on pyridostigmine.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: All patients with newly diagnosed myasthenia need a CT chest to look for a thymoma in the anterior mediastinum, which would need thymectomy.

steps.x: Next test after confirming myasthenia.
Every new myasthenic needs a search for a thymoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT chest**.

elim: There is no cardiac indication.
Brain imaging does not change MG management.
Biopsy is for myopathy, not NMJ disease.
TFTs screen for autoimmune thyroid disease; ultrasound is not routine.

steps.x: **A. CT chest.** New MG = CT chest for thymoma.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has fatigable ptosis and diplopia. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive and CT chest is normal. She has no breathing or swallowing difficulty.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Pyridostigmine, a long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is first line. Immunosuppression is added for persistent symptoms; IVIG and plasma exchange are for crisis.

steps.x: Initial treatment in stable, newly diagnosed myasthenia.
Confirmed MG, no thymoma, no crisis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pyridostigmine**.

elim: Azathioprine is a second-line, steroid-sparing agent.
IVIG is for crisis.
Plasma exchange is for crisis.
There is no thymoma; thymectomy is not the initial step.

steps.x: **D. Pyridostigmine.** First-line MG = pyridostigmine.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man with myasthenia gravis has a 3 day history of increasing breathlessness and difficulty swallowing. His pulse rate is 116 bpm, BP 140/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. His forced vital capacity has fallen to 1.1 L. He has been reviewed by the intensive care team and is being supported on the ward.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
practice.e: Myasthenic crisis needs admission and respiratory support, then IVIG or plasmapheresis as definitive treatment. Azathioprine is too slow and gentamicin worsens MG.

steps.x: Definitive treatment of myasthenic crisis, once respiratory support is arranged.

clues: reviewed by the intensive care team
steps.x: Myasthenic crisis with falling FVC; airway already addressed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV immunoglobulin** (or plasmapheresis).

elim: More pyridostigmine risks cholinergic crisis and does not remove antibodies.
Aminoglycosides worsen myasthenia.
Azathioprine takes months to work.
Thymectomy is elective, never during a crisis.

steps.x: **C. IV immunoglobulin.** Crisis = respiratory support + IVIG or plasma exchange.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman with generalised myasthenia gravis is well controlled on pyridostigmine. CT chest shows a 4 cm anterior mediastinal mass consistent with a thymoma.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Thymectomy is the definitive treatment, particularly when a thymoma is present, as the thymus drives autoantibody production.

steps.x: Definitive management with a thymoma.

clues: anterior mediastinal mass consistent with a thymoma
steps.x: MG with thymoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thymectomy**.

elim: Radiotherapy is adjuvant, not the primary treatment.
Steroids treat symptoms but leave the thymoma.
